activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: A primary source was produced at the time being studied, such as a letter or diary, while a secondary source, such as a textbook, interprets the past later using primary sources.
story:
Justin had until four o'clock, when the library closed, and the essay was due at eight the next morning. The topic his teacher had assigned, why historians disagree about the same past, seemed designed to punish him. He had three hours and a stack of his grandfather's letters that his mother had pressed on him that morning, saying only, "Take these. There might be something in them."

He spread the letters across the study table by the window. They were written on thin blue airmail paper, dated across four years of a war Justin knew mostly from a textbook chapter he had half-read in September. The handwriting slanted and cramped at the ends of pages, as though paper itself were rationed. Beside them he set the textbook, its spine uncracked, its chapter titled with a calm authority the letters did not share.

Magalie slid into the chair across from him, dropping her bag. "You look like you're smuggling something."

"Kind of." He turned a letter so she could see. "My grandfather wrote these during the war. To my grandmother. And the textbook says the thing he's describing here didn't happen the way he says."

She pulled the letter closer, scanning it. "So he lied?"

"I don't think he lied." Justin tapped the page. "He wrote it the day after. But he was one guy, on one ship, seeing one piece of it."

Magalie turned the letter over, then looked at the textbook. "My brother's in college," she said. "He talks about this constantly. The letters are primary sources. A primary source was made at the time, by someone who was there. The textbook is a secondary source. It interprets the past later, using primary sources like these." She said it the way she repeated anything her brother said, half-showing off, half not believing she got to be the one who knew.

"So neither one is just true." Justin stacked the letters, then unstacked them. "The textbook author read letters like these and decided what they added up to. And another historian could read the same ones and add them up differently." His grandfather's handwriting ran in lines that crossed out their own certainties, one sentence correcting the one before it.

Mr. Virtanen passed their table with a cart of returns and paused. "Those are airmail, aren't they. We don't see those much anymore." He adjusted his glasses but did not reach for the letters, which Justin was quietly glad of, the way you're glad when an adult doesn't take over the thing you're figuring out. "The microfilm room is open until we close, if you want newspapers from that period. Though the reader's been obdurate all week. You have to hit the advance pedal twice."

"Everything here has a deadline," Magalie said.

"The library amortized the cost of that reader over fifteen years," Mr. Virtanen said, pushing the cart on. "It plans to outlive all of us."

In the microfilm room, Justin fed the reel and hit the pedal twice, and the newspaper pages jumped under the glass. The war looked different here again, filtered through censors and deadlines and the need to sell papers the next morning. A story on the front page gave a number of ships; his grandfather's letter gave a different number; the textbook gave a third, with a footnote. Three versions, each produced at a different distance from the event, each answering a different question, because the newspaper wanted to know what happened yesterday, the textbook wanted to know what it meant, and his grandfather, as far as Justin could tell, mostly wanted to tell a nineteen-year-old girl that he was still alive.

On his way back through the stacks, he passed the philosophy section and a fat spine reading Phenomenology: The Study of Experience as It Is Lived. He didn't pull it out, but the phrase stayed with him, because that was what the letters were, wasn't it, experience as it was lived, with no view of the whole.

He sat down, opened his laptop, and typed the first sentence of the essay: Historians disagree about the past because no one was everywhere, and every source, made at the time or written long after, holds only the piece its maker could see. He read it over. It was not wrong, exactly. But it left out the part he was least sure of, the part where his grandfather's number and the textbook's number might both be honest and both be mistaken. He typed a second sentence, deleted it, typed it again.

At 3:55 the overhead lights blinked twice. Magalie zipped her bag and stood. "You done?"

"Close enough." Justin gathered the letters, squared them against the table edge, and slid them back into the folder his mother had given him. One corner of the top letter stuck out, and he could see the last line his grandfather had written, the ink faded to the color of weak tea. He pushed it back in, picked up the folder, and followed her toward the doors as the lights blinked a third time.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
Amelia had chosen the playground because it was empty after seven, and because the bench under the climbing frame felt less like a waiting room than her kitchen table did. She spread the application form on her knees, the crease from her back pocket running through the word availability like a scar. Corbin arrived carrying two gas station coffees and his mother's old blazer, which hung off his shoulders the way weather hangs off a mountain.

"You're the interviewer," she said. "Be terrible. Be realistic."

Corbin sat on the swing beside her, set his coffee on the rubber matting, and drew his face into something bored and institutional. "Why do you want to work at Bellamy's Hardware?"

"Because I need money for textbooks," Amelia said, and then, hearing it land flat, watched a jogger pass the fence while she tried again. "Because I like knowing how things work, and I'm good with people when they're frustrated." She looked at Corbin's ear instead of his eyes. He wrote something on his palm with his finger, which she knew meant no.

Julie had told her over lunch that eye contact was a talent you either had or pathologized in yourself for lacking, and Amelia had spent two days deciding that was the kind of sophistry that sounds wise in a cafeteria. Either it was a skill, learnable like anything else, or it wasn't, and she intended to find out which. That was the point of the playground, of the blazer, of the three mornings she had answered questions into her phone's voice recorder and flinched at the playback.

"Grandpa says the handshake matters more than anything," Corbin said, dropping the interviewer face. "He made me practise for an hour before my library interview. He told me about this study he read, from 2000, some psychologist named William Chaplin. It found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions." He offered his hand, palm damp, grip like a wet cloth. "Obviously I failed his lesson."

"So grip harder."

"It's not just harder, it's, like, committed. He said a dead-fish handshake tells them you'll be a dead-fish employee." Corbin laughed at his own grandpa, then stopped laughing when Amelia didn't. "Sorry. Do it again."

She took his hand. The first attempt was too hard, a performance of firmness that made him wince, and the second was too apologetic, and on the third she stopped thinking about her hand at all because she was looking at his face, actually looking, and the grip settled into something neither of them had to think about. "That," Corbin said, and shook his fingers out. "That one. Do you want to know something stupid? My library interview, the whole time I was so busy doing the handshake right that I forgot to answer the second question."

Amelia considered this. She had been thinking of the interview as a list of fixed techniques, the handshake, the eye contact, the clear answers, each one a lever she could pull, and Corbin's failure suggested the levers were connected in ways the list didn't show. Maybe attention was a single substance and you could only spend it in one place. Maybe confidence wasn't a mask you put on but a budget you allocated. She did not like either possibility, because both meant that practise could only take her so far and the rest would be her, unarmored, in a chair across from a stranger.

Ms. Nguyen, who walked her terrier past the playground every evening and had, Amelia knew, managed the bookshop on Fenwick Street for eleven years, paused at the gate and watched them shake hands for the fourth time. "Job interview?" she said, and when Amelia nodded, she came in and sat on the end of the slide's ladder, her terrier sniffing at the rubber matting. "Ask her the hard one," she said to Corbin, as though they had planned it. "Ask her where she sees herself in five years."

Corbin asked it, bored-voiced again. Amelia met his eyes and said, "Honest answer, in college, and working somewhere that isn't hardware, but working hard at it anyway," and Ms. Nguyen laughed, one short note, and said the honesty would do more for her than the answer would. Then Ms. Nguyen asked whether the coffee was hers to steal, and took Corbin's without waiting, and Amelia sat with her hand still remembering the shape of a handshake she could not fully explain, and Ms. Nguyen said, "Now stand up. You're slouching like the bench is hedonistic and you've surrendered to it."

Amelia stood. She smoothed the crease out of the application form with the heel of her hand, and the paper held the line anyway.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, 'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.'
story:
The library smelled like the heater had been running all weekend, and Landon had spread his copy of The Catcher in the Rye across two chairs so that no one would sit near him. He needed the whole table, or at least he told himself he did. The essay prompt was on the board in his head the way Mr. Cho had written it: How does point of view shape what we believe? And underneath it, the thing Mr. Cho had said to him after class on Friday, quietly, with the door still open: I want to talk to you Monday about your last essay.

David dropped his backpack on the far chair anyway. "You look like a hostage."

"I'm fine."

"You've read the same page four times. I watched you."

Sheldon arrived with two milks from the vending machine and gave one to David without being asked, which was how Sheldon did most things. He was the most taciturn person in their grade, but he had a way of showing up exactly when a conversation needed a third voice. He sat down and read the prompt off Landon's notebook, upside down. "Unreliable narrator," he said.

"Right." Landon turned the book around and pushed it across the table. "Page thirty-eight. Read it."

David read it aloud in a flat voice, the way he read everything, even stuff that deserved better. "'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life. It's awful.'" He looked up. "So the book was published in 1951, and this kid tells you straight out that he lies. That's the whole problem, isn't it. What do we even believe after that?"

"Mr. Cho asked us that on day one," Sheldon said. "How much of Holden's story to believe after he admits he lies."

Landon had written nothing down on day one. That was the fact he hadn't told either of them, the fact he was circling. His last essay, the one Mr. Cho wanted to talk about, had been about a book he hadn't finished, and he had done it smoothly enough that he'd almost believed it himself. He had invented a scene in chapter twenty-two and built his whole argument on it, and Mr. Cho had written one line in the margin, in red, in his small careful handwriting: Whose voice is this? He hadn't written anything else. No grade. Just that.

"Here's what I keep getting stuck on," Landon said, and he pulled the book back and turned pages without looking at them, buying time. "If he says he lies, does that make him more honest or less? Like, a liar who admits it is giving you a warning label. But he could be lying about being a liar."

"That problematizes everything," David said, pleased with himself. "Every single thing he tells us."

"That's not a complication, that's the whole point," Sheldon said, and for once he kept going, which was how Landon knew they'd hit something real. "The narrator picks what to tell you. Holden's the one standing between you and everything that happened. Even when he's honest, you only get his side." He peeled the foil off his milk. "It's like a proof. You have a lemma, something you prove first so you can use it later. He proves he lies early on, and then everything after that depends on it."

Landon stopped turning pages. He sat with his hand flat on the cover. He was thinking about the essay again, and about how Mr. Cho's one line in red had seemed, at first, like a lucky escape, like the teacher had merely been asking about style. But now, with the book under his hand, the question had changed shape. Whose voice is this? Holden would have known the answer. Holden would have made up something terrific.

"So what's the essay going to say?" David asked.

Landon looked at the page number where a kid in 1951 had admitted to being the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life, and then he closed the book and squared it on the table. "That you can't trust him and you can't throw him out either. That the admission doesn't solve anything. It just means you have to read everything twice."

"That sounds hard to grade," David said.

"I'm going to write it honestly." Landon slid his chair back. "All of it."

He left the book with them and walked through the rows of shelves toward the front desk, where Mr. Cho happened to be checking out a stack of returns, and Landon stood there a second with his essay folder in his hand before he set it on the counter. "There's a part I made up," he said. "Chapter twenty-two. Before you ask me Monday."

Mr. Cho looked at the folder, then at him, and slid a blank sheet of paper across the counter.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
Aaron had spread his biology notes across the kitchen table in an order that was supposed to mean something, and by eleven it meant nothing. The unit test was first period. His mother had gone to bed with the door shut, and the only sounds were the refrigerator and the pen he kept clicking against his teeth. At the top of the page he had written the plan, three words he'd copied off the board: replication, transcription, translation. He understood replication. The other two had dissolved somewhere between the classroom and this table.

His phone buzzed. Rogan, from his grandmother's house in Norway, where the family had gone for the week.

"How's the studying," the message said. "I'm dead here. She talks for four hours straight."

"Fine," Aaron typed, which was a lie, and then, because it was Rogan, he sent a second message that was true: "I don't get translation. Like actually don't get it."

Rogan sent back a photograph: grey water, a cliff going straight down into it, his own sneakers in the foreground on a wet rock. "This fjord is the only thing keeping me sane," the caption read. "Also there's a goat." Aaron looked at it for a long moment, the cold of the water almost coming through the screen, then put the phone face-down.

He tried to codify what he knew into a list, numbered, orderly, the way Mr. Chan kept telling them to do. One: DNA unzips. Two: a copy is made, the messenger RNA, which carries the instructions out of the nucleus. That part he could say out loud without stumbling. Three: and here the list broke down, because the textbook's diagram showed a large grey blob on the mRNA strand with amino acids floating toward it, and Aaron could not see what the blob did. He had assumed, on first reading, that the protein was assembled first and the blob read it afterward, checking it, the way a teacher walks the rows after a test. He'd written that in his notes. He'd written it confidently, with an underline.

He pulled up the email Mr. Chan had sent the whole class on Friday. "If translation confuses you, study the diagram, not the summary paragraph. Watch what moves. Watch what joins." No more than that. Aaron read it twice, annoyed, and then got down on his elbows with his nose close to the page.

The blob had a label. Ribosome. There was an arrow on the mRNA, pointing along it, and the ribosome sat on the strand like a hand on a zipper. Aaron sat very still. In his grandmother's jewelry box, which his mother kept on the shelf in the hallway, there was a necklace she had strung herself at a craft fair: a hand sliding beads onto thread, reading the pattern off a card in her lap, one bead at a time. She hadn't built the necklace and then read it. She read as she went. He got up, went to the hallway, and brought the necklace back to the table, the beads clicking faintly against each other in his palm. The ribosome moved along the messenger RNA and joined the amino acids together as it went, building the chain link by link. He found the word for the joins in the caption at the bottom of the diagram. Peptide bonds.

"Wait," he said out loud, to nobody, and crossed out the underlined sentence in his notes so hard the pen went through the paper.

He called Haydn, who answered on the second ring with the TV going in the background.

"You still up," Aaron said.

"Obviously. What."

"Tell me what you have for translation. The actual thing the ribosome does."

Haydn paused. "It, like, reads the mRNA."

"And?"

"That's what I wrote."

"You have the diagram? Page 212. Look at it and tell me what's happening to the amino acids while the ribosome reads."

He heard Haydn's chair scrape, pages turning. The TV went quiet. On the table the necklace lay in a coil, and Aaron slid it toward himself with one finger, thinking that if he could not say it tomorrow in a full sentence, under Mr. Chan's flat stare, the diagram would not save him.

"Oh," Haydn said. "Oh, it's threading them. It's moving along and stringing them together while it goes."

"With peptide bonds," Aaron said. "Say that part too. He'll ask for the exact word."

"For a moribund student body at eleven at night," Haydn said, "we are being remarkably useful to each other."

"Page 212," Aaron said again, and opened his notebook to a clean sheet.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns during the president's ten-day window and the president does not sign the bill, so it does not become law.
story:
Gabriel set his phone face down beside his plate, which his mother had told him a hundred times not to do, and pushed rice around until it formed a low ridge along the rim. His father asked how the physics test had gone. Gabriel said fine, which was true, and then said nothing for a while, which his parents pretended not to notice. On the phone, face down, was a photograph of a worksheet. He had taken it because he could not stop looking at it, and looking at it at dinner felt less like rudeness than like carrying something.

"It's this civics thing," he finally said, when his mother asked why he was eating like a man serving a sentence. "We had this question in class today. Mr. Sato gave us a bill that passed both houses, went to the president, and then just died. Nobody vetoed it. The president never said no. It just ended."

His father, who sold insurance and believed every problem was a paperwork problem, put down his fork. "Bills don't die of natural causes."

"That's what Eshaan said." Gabriel turned the phone over and slid it beside the salt so his father could see the worksheet, the timeline with its empty box where the veto should have been. "Eshaan thought the president must have vetoed it secretly, which, no. Nelson thought it was a typo in the textbook. Mr. Sato just kept smiling like the answer was a party he wasn't going to invite us to. He said, figure out what Congress was doing during those ten days, and that was the only hint we got."

"Ten days," his mother repeated. She was a nurse and counted things for a living, days since surgery, days of medication, days until discharge. "Ten days to do what?"

"Sign it, or veto it. That's the window. If the president doesn't sign and Congress is still there, it becomes law anyway. That part we learned weeks ago. The bill can pass without him." Gabriel drew the two paths in the air with his chopsticks, one line arcing toward law, one toward veto. "But this bill, the one on the worksheet, it just stopped. And Mr. Sato's hint was about Congress, not the president, which is the part that doesn't make sense. The bill isn't Congress's anymore. It's on the president's desk."

His sister, who was eleven and believed dinner was a venue for tattling, said he was being boring. His father told her to eat. The kitchen went quiet in that particular way, the exhaust fan ticking, and Gabriel sat with the strange feeling he sometimes got in math class, where a problem refused to be parametrized, where he could not find the variable that made the whole thing move. Then, still holding the chopsticks, he did find it.

"Unless Congress went home," he said. "Adjourned. Like, ended their session." He was speaking faster now, half standing, and his mother told him to sit. "Think about it. If Congress is in session and the president ignores the bill, it becomes law without him. But if they've adjourned, there's nobody there to receive it. Nobody to override anything. The bill just sits there on his desk for the whole ten days and then the session's over and it never comes back." He looked from his mother to his father. "He doesn't sign it. He doesn't say no. It just dies because they left."

"Is that legal?" his father asked.

"It has to be. It's in the worksheet." Gabriel picked the phone back up and scrolled, and there it was in the fine print at the bottom of the page, a phrase he had skimmed past twice. He read it out loud: "It's called a pocket veto." He said it twice more, quieter, the way he memorized vocabulary, and then he laughed, one syllable, mostly at himself. "It was in the footnotes the whole time. He put it in the footnotes."

His mother said it sounded like a loophole, and there was something in her voice that made Gabriel pause, because in her milieu, her intensive care unit, a loophole was never a neutral thing; it was how a hospital discharged a patient nobody had decided about. His father, though, was shaking his head slowly, the way he did when a client insisted a policy covered something it did not. "No," he said. "Think about what a veto is. A veto is the president saying no and Congress getting a chance to fight back, to override him. This way, the president never has to fight. He just has to wait. That's not a loophole. That's the whole knife." He stabbed a piece of broccoli to demonstrate, and his sister giggled, and he didn't notice.

Gabriel had spent the walk home drafting a message to Mr. Sato arguing that the textbook was wrong, that a bill could not simply vanish, and now he was glad he hadn't sent it. It had seemed to him at lunch, when Nelson was being particularly trenchant about lazy textbook editors, that the world of the civics class was clean, that a bill either climbed the whole ladder, committee to floor to both houses to signature, or was pushed off it by an honest no. That was the story he had wanted the system to tell. But the system also had quiet rooms in it, and empty desks, and a bill lying on a desk in an adjourned Capitol while the ten days ran out like water.

He wasn't sure yet whether he thought the pocket veto was clever or rotten. Both, probably, and he would have to sit with that, because Mr. Sato would ask them tomorrow and would not want a verdict; he would want the reasoning. Gabriel took his plate to the sink, then went back for his phone, and standing in the doorway he typed the message he would actually send: So the president can just wait them out. That's the answer, right? Footnote three.

He read it over once, thumb hovering, and sent it.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The newspaper arrived with the morning bread, and Henry's father set it beside his plate without ceremony, which was itself a kind of ceremony. They were ten days into the trip, ten days of his aunt's apartment in Marseille with its shutters that banged in the wind, and every morning the paper came and every morning Henry ignored it, until that morning he could not. Mr. Lee, who lived two floors down and had once corrected proofs at the local paper for thirty years, had promised him a tour of the newsroom, but only on one condition, stated over espresso on the balcony with his thin hands folded: Henry would read one article, a full one, and summarize it aloud, in French, in front of him.

Henry had studied French for three years, which was enough to order fish and not enough to read a newspaper, and he had four days. He took the paper to the sea wall where his classmates from the exchange program had gathered, Cristina with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair and Charles-Emile lying on the concrete with his hat over his face. Cristina found the whole project hilarious in a way that was not unkind. "Which article?" she asked, and when Henry shrugged she flipped through and stabbed a finger at a long piece about a tunnel project under the old port, six paragraphs dense as wet sand.

He started at the end. It seemed like strategy: the last paragraph was shortest, and he had some idea that the ending would tell him what the article was about, the way the last line of a novel did. He worked through it word by word with his pocket dictionary, sweating, and after forty minutes he knew only that some official had thanked some committee. Charles-Emile lifted the brim of his hat and watched him suffer for a while before speaking. "You're doing it backwards," he said. "Most news articles use the inverted pyramid: the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story." Cristina nodded along as if this were a maxim everyone was born knowing, and Henry felt the blood climb his face, because he had spent an evening on the wrong end of the article.

He went back to the beginning anyway, to check. The first paragraph, which he had skimmed assuming it was throat-clearing, held nearly everything: what had been approved, by whom, for how much money, what would be built and when the work would start. Everything after it was quotation, dispute, history, texture. He tested this against a second article and a third, holding the paper up like a machine he had been using incorrectly for years, and the pattern held. The last paragraphs were the least load-bearing, the garnish and not the meal. He read the tunnel article's opening six times until the sentences sat in his mouth instead of in front of his eyes.

On the appointed evening he climbed down two flights with the folded paper damp in his hand. Mr. Lee's apartment smelled of typewriter ribbon and anise. There was a small table, two chairs, a lamp angled like an interrogation lamp in a film, and on the wall a framed front page that Henry glanced at only once, because the date made something turn over in him and he cauterized the thought before it could spread. Later, he told himself. Read first. He chose the article, laid it flat, smoothed the crease with the side of his hand.

"Whenever you are ready," Mr. Lee said, and poured himself a glass of water, unhurried, as though Henry's success or failure were weather to him.

Henry read the opening paragraph aloud. His voice caught twice on consonant clusters that did not exist in English, and he heard his own errors the way one hears a wrong note played on purpose. But the structure held him up. When he lost the thread of a clause he knew it did not matter, because the clause was a detail; when he stumbled over the third paragraph he skipped it whole and Mr. Lee's expression did not change. Then he closed the paper, or nearly closed it, and gave the summary: the project, the amount, the two years of work, the opposition from the merchants' association. It took under a minute. He had expected to drown and instead had learned to swim in the shallow end first, where the water was, because that was where the water was.

Mr. Lee was quiet long enough that the fridge hummed into the silence. Then he stood, took the framed front page down from the wall, and set it on the table in front of Henry. The date was from before Henry was born. The byline, small and steady, was his mother's name.

"She sat where you will sit tomorrow," Mr. Lee said. "The tour is at nine o'clock. Bring the paper if you like. You read it better than she did, her first time. She also started at the end."

Henry looked at the name for a long moment, then at the lamp, then at the door.

"Can I keep this?" he asked. "Just for tonight."

Mr. Lee slid the frame across the table.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
Makayla had taped her ten tree paintings above the sink, in the order she had made them, and by second period she already wanted to take half of them down. The tree stood in the corner of Eliza's yard, a maple whose branches split low, and she had painted it at dawn, at noon, at dusk, in rain, in October light and in the flat grey of March. Ms. Tran wanted the portfolio finished by Friday, theme and statement included, and the theme was the one part Makayla had never doubted until now.

"Is it enough?" she asked Gael, who was glazing a coil pot two tables away and had opinions about everything. "Like, is it variety, or is it just the same thing ten times?"

Gael wiped his hands and looked. He took longer than she expected, walking the length of the row, tilting his head at the dawn one, then the dusk. "It's not the same thing," he said finally. "It's the same thing under different light. You know Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year. Same facade. Nobody says he was lazy."

"Thirty," Makayla said. She did the arithmetic against her ten and felt both relieved and annoyed, the way she did whenever a solution arrived by way of someone else's example. The art world liked to lionize Monet for exactly the thing she was afraid would count against her, and she could not decide whether that proved her idea was good or proved that the idea only worked if you were already Monet.

Eliza came in at lunch with a sandwich and bad news delivered gently, which was Eliza's way. "My dad's taking the maple down," she said. "The roots are in the septic line. He's got a guy coming Saturday." She must have seen something move in Makayla's face, because she set the sandwich down and added, "I didn't know how to tell you. I thought maybe you were done."

Makayla looked at the row of paintings and understood that she had been thinking of the tree as hers, which was a kind of parasitism she hadn't named until that moment. The tree had existed for forty years before she needed it. She had taken its light and its weather and called the whole transaction a theme. "I have two blank canvases at home," she said. "Can I come tomorrow, really early? Before school?"

They sat on Eliza's porch steps at six-forty, coats over pajamas, and the tree came up out of the dark the way it always did, branch by branch. The dawn light that day was turbid, pooled and yellowish under low cloud, and Makayla painted fast, the way she could only paint when the subject was about to be taken from her. Eliza drank tea beside her and said nothing, which was its own kind of help, and once she reached over and moved the palette out of the path of a drip from the porch roof.

The second canvas she saved for after school, and the tree was different again in the flat afternoon light, more ordinary, less dramatic, and she understood suddenly that the drama had never been the point. Her statement drafts kept circling the word transformation, but what she actually had was persistence, one thing looked at again and again because looking was all she could do for it. She thought of the cathedral facade, whatever it had looked like, standing there through two years of Monet's mornings while the painter decided, over and over, that it was worth one more.

On Saturday morning she went back with the camera on her phone, because Eliza had asked whether she wanted a record, and Makayla had said yes before she finished thinking. The crew arrived with ropes and a chipper. She stood at the edge of the yard, and when the first branch came down, crashing through the lower limbs, she lifted the phone and held it steady, framing the tree against the sky for the last of its mornings.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
The rehearsal space smelled of dust and old paint, the ghost of productions nobody had swept away. Maelle stood at the folding table she had claimed as her director's station, a photocopied script open to the page where she had penciled her embryonic blocking notes, arrows and X's that looked, in the flat light, like a plan for a battle that had not begun. The one-act was hers to direct because Mr. Tesfaye, who ran the community theatre's winter workshop, had looked at the sign-up sheet and said, "We have eleven actors and no directors under forty. Take the slot." She had said yes before she understood what yes would cost her.

"Okay," she said. "Top of scene two. David, you enter left."

David, who had played a narrator in the fall showcase and considered himself beyond instruction, walked in from the wrong wing. Miya, standing at her mark near the false fireplace, watched him cross the entire stage in the wrong direction and then stop, waiting.

"No, your other left," Maelle said, and David reversed, and Miya laughed, and the whole thing collapsed into the kind of shuffling that passes for a break when nobody has called one.

It happened twice more that afternoon. David entered wrong, Miya compensated by drifting off her mark, and Maelle felt her authority leaking out of her like air from a slow tire. She had wanted this. She had a folder of notes on the play's rhythm, on what the second monologue needed, and none of it mattered because she could not get two people to walk through a door in the right order. She thought of blaming the confusion on happenstance, the casual accident of a first rehearsal, but she knew it was not an accident. She was saying a word and the word meant something she did not know.

After the others left, she stayed. Mr. Tesfaye was locking the prop cabinet in the corner, unhurried, keys jingling. She did not ask him. Instead she walked down off the stage, crossed the empty house, and sat in the third row of folding chairs, where an audience would sit. Then she walked back up, stood where David had stood, and faced out the way an actor faces.

"Left," she said to the empty room, and her arm went toward the wing David had used. Then she came back to the seats and looked at the stage, and her arm went the other way, toward the opposite side. She did this four times, like a person checking a locked door. From the seats, the side she called left was on her right. From the stage, they had traded places, and the names belonged to the actor, not to her.

She found Mr. Tesfaye by the light board. "Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience," she said. "So they're the reverse of the audience's left and right."

"Did you look that up, or did you figure it out?" he asked.

"I sat in the audience and raised my arm a lot," she said. He almost smiled and went back to his switches.

The next rehearsal, she taped the floor before anyone arrived, wrote SL on one strip and SR on the other, large enough to read from the back row of the house. When David arrived she said, "You enter stage left, which for you is the wing on your left. I'll call it that from now on, and I'll call it from your side, not mine." He looked at the tape, looked at the wings, and this time he came in where she wanted him to, and Miya did not have to drift anywhere to meet him.

The scene ran. It was rough, half the pace it needed, David stepping on Miya's cue line twice, but the shape of it held, and Maelle began to see what she had imagined in her folder happening in three dimensions, imperfect and alive. What she had not settled, even in her own head, was how much to fix and how much to let the actors find. Miya wanted to talk through her monologue; David wanted to be told. Two people, one stage, and she was beginning to think directing meant holding both approaches at once rather than choosing, though she could not yet say whether that was wisdom or just indecision dressed up. She let Miya talk and gave David an arrow on the tape, and both seemed, for one run-through, satisfied.

On the last night of the workshop, after the one-act had been performed for thirty-two people, Miya found her in the lobby. "The second monologue," Miya said. "You didn't change it. I thought you would."

"I thought about it every rehearsal," Maelle said.

"So why didn't you?"

Maelle looked past her at the stage door, propped open, the taped marks still visible under the work lights. "Because when you finally said it tonight, it was yours." Miya nodded slowly, then pulled her into a hug that smelled like hairspray and cold air from the loading dock, and over her shoulder Maelle watched the stage crew strike the fireplace, carrying it off toward stage left.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homophily, a term from sociologists Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton in 1954, is the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves.
story:
The truck smelled like cardboard and old carpet, and Jonathan had been alone with that smell for an hour before the box marked WINTER STUFF began to sneeze. He pulled onto the shoulder, heart going like a drum solo, and peeled back the flap to find Mylee folded between his coats with a granola bar and a look of total innocence.

"You kidnapped yourself," he said.

"I liberated myself." She climbed out and stretched, popping something in her shoulder. "Kendra was supposed to come but she chickened out, so I'm representing the whole friendship. Both halves. Me and the empty space where you used to sit."

He laughed despite himself, or maybe because of it, and let her ride shotgun the last forty miles, feet on the dash, narrating the billboards like a nature documentary. Here we observe the personal injury lawyer in his native habitat. She was doing this because she was funny, obviously, but also because she was stalling, and they both knew the clock on the dash was counting down the same minutes.

Last spring, after the college acceptances had come and gone and it was settled that Jonathan's family was moving in June, he had gone to Mr. Ramos after class to argue his way out of caring. Mr. Ramos had refused to lecture him, which was typical, and had instead handed him a paperback and said only, "Read the marked page and tell me what you think." The marked page was about two sociologists, Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton, who in 1954 gave a name to the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves. Jonathan had read it on the bus and then texted Mylee a single question mark, and she had texted back a shrugging emoji, and he had thought about it every day since, usually while watching the lunchroom arrange itself like iron filings around a magnet. Band kids with band kids, runners with runners, the quiet ones finding each other by some silent auction.

"Homophily," he said now, apropos of a billboard for a housing development called The Meadows at Cedar Grove.

"Bless you," said Mylee.

"It's that thing from the Ramos book. Lazarsfeld and Merton, 1954. People form ties with people similar to themselves. I've decided it's the enemy."

"You've decided a fact is the enemy."

"Facts can be on the wrong side." He gripped the wheel. "The whole point of moving somewhere new is that you get shuffled into a deck of strangers. But if everybody just snaps together with their own kind, the runners find the runners, the gamers find the gamers, and I show up with no kind at all. It's like a party where everyone's already dancing."

Mylee unwrapped her granola bar with the deliberateness of a person preparing to win an argument. "First of all, you have a kind. You're the guy who reads sociology for fun and worries at it like a dog with a bone. You'll find the other dogs within a week. Second, you're acting like friendship is some altruistic gift you bestow, when really you just commodify it, you collect people like trading cards, and now you're worried the new set won't have your favorites. Third, and most devastating, Kendra bet me five dollars you'd say exactly this before we hit the county line, so hand it over."

He fished a crumpled five from his hoodie pocket and she took it with the probity of a bank teller, counting it twice and tucking it away for Kendra, and they were both laughing, hard enough that he had to slow down, and somewhere in the middle of the laughing he understood that his position had two halves and he was allowed to hold both. The sociologists were right, people did cluster, and that was not a tragedy but a current you could swim in; and also the ties he already had were not going to dissolve just because a fact described their ordinary behavior. He did not know how much of the second half was true. He decided, for the first time all summer, that not knowing was livable.

"So what's the plan," Mylee said, as the exit for his new town came up green and inevitable. "You going to be one of those kids who sits alone for a month out of principle?"

"The principle of style, maybe. Brooding is a look."

"It's a bad look." She pointed at the exit. "Take this one. My turn's the next one over."

He glanced at her. "Your turn."

"Dad got the transfer in April. We're eleven miles from your new house." She was already pulling out her phone to text Kendra. "I was going to tell you at the truck, but honestly, watching you monologue about sociology was worth the wait."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, a landlord may collect a rent deposit of no more than one month's rent, or one rent period if rent is paid more often, but may not charge a damage deposit.
story:
Peyton sat on an overturned milk crate in Graham's garage, a clipboard on her knees and two leases side by side on the workbench, because Graham's mother had claimed the kitchen table for a puzzle with, apparently, no end date. The garage smelled of motor oil and the ghost of old cigarettes. A space heater ticked in the corner like something trying to resuscitate itself.

"Read it again," Aleena said, perched on the hood of the lawnmower. "The part about the deposit."

Peyton found the clause in the second lease, the one for the apartment above the laundromat on Carling. "A damage deposit of one thousand two hundred dollars shall be paid prior to occupancy." She read it flat, the way you read something so you can hear how wrong it sounds.

"That's a lot," Graham said. "That's basically another month."

"That's exactly another month. Rent's twelve hundred." Peyton set the clipboard down and pulled out her phone. She had a heuristic for moments like this, inherited from her father: if a number in a contract makes your stomach drop, someone, somewhere, has already written down whether it's allowed. Her father had used it for a tow bill once and gotten half of it back. It had never failed her, though it had never made her popular.

She typed Ontario damage deposit into the search bar and scrolled past a forum where a landlord called a tenant "the cancer of this building." Then she found a plain page, government-branded, dull as a textbook. She read it twice. "Okay," she said. "So in Ontario a landlord can collect a rent deposit. But only up to one month's rent. Or one rent period, if you pay rent more often than monthly." She scrolled. "But they can't charge a damage deposit. At all."

Aleena slid off the lawnmower. "So this whole clause is illegal?"

"Not illegal, exactly. I don't know what it is. I know it's not allowed." Peyton was careful about the difference, even though she couldn't have explained it. "It says they can ask for the rent deposit, one month, held for the last month. But the damage deposit part, they just can't ask for that."

Graham leaned over her shoulder, breathing garlicky chips onto her screen. "So you just tell them no?"

"I tell them I know they can't ask for it," Peyton said. "Which is different from telling them no. Telling them no sounds like an opinion."

The first lease, the one for the room in Aleena's cousin's house near campus, had no deposit at all but utilities that weren't included, and Peyton had spent an hour building a table on the clipboard: rent, hydro estimate, internet, the laundromat versus in-suite difference, the bus pass she'd need at one place and not the other. The numbers came out within nine dollars of each other, which felt almost gratuitous, like the universe refusing to help her decide. The Carling apartment was brighter and had a dishwasher. The room in the house had Aleena's cousin, who was apparently "fine, mostly."

She called the number on the Carling lease from the doorway of the garage, where the reception was one bar better. A man answered on the fourth ring, mid-chew.

"Hi, I'm interested in the apartment on Carling. I had a question about the deposit clause." She kept her voice flat, pleasant, the voice of someone reading from a page, which she was. "In Ontario, a landlord can collect a rent deposit of up to one month's rent, or one rent period if rent's paid more often, but can't charge a damage deposit. So I wanted to ask about the twelve hundred listed here."

There was a long silence with chewing in it. Then: "That's standard. Everyone pays it."

"Is it the rent deposit? Because the lease already lists last month's rent separately."

Another silence. The chewing stopped. "Let me call you back," he said, and hung up before she could say anything else, which Peyton decided to interpret as progress.

She went back inside and sat on the crate. Aleena had migrated to the space heater and was holding her hands over it like a small religious painting. Graham had drawn a mustache on the landlord's printed name.

"He'll either drop it or rent to someone who doesn't ask," Peyton said. "And I can't know which until he calls back. That's the part I hate."

"So you'd take the apartment? Over the room?"

"I'd take the apartment if the numbers were honest. The room's numbers are honest and boring. The apartment's numbers are dishonest and have a dishwasher." She looked at the table on her clipboard, the two columns with their nine-dollar difference, and at the phone face-up on the workbench beside a jar of mismatched screws. "I don't know. I actually don't know. The room above the laundromat is better if he fixes it, and worse if he's like this about everything."

The phone buzzed against the workbench and skittered half an inch toward the jar. Peyton picked it up and read the screen.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
The error message had been on the screen for eleven minutes when Eli finally read it out loud. "Book.java line twenty. Title has private access in Book." He was sitting at the kitchen table with his laptop open and his textbook propped against the fruit bowl, and outside the window the streetlight had just come on, that early purple kind of evening where the inside of the house felt warmer than it was.

He had written the class exactly the way the assignment sheet described: a private field called title, a constructor, a getter. The trouble was the test. Ms. Kapoor wanted three lines in the main method proving the object worked, and his proof kept dissolving into red text. He typed it again, slower this time, letting his fingers recalibrate to the fact that the problem might not be a typo. Book myBook equals new Book, quotes, "The Grapes of Wrath". Then the line that broke everything: System.out.println, myBook dot title. Red again. Same message, same line.

Kaiden arrived at six with his backpack still on, having texted from the driveway. He pulled a chair around backward and sat with his arms folded across the back of it, studying the screen over Eli's shoulder the way people study a chessboard after someone has already made the wrong move. "You're doing it right," he said. "Except you're doing it wrong."

"Thanks. Very helpful."

"No, look." Kaiden leaned in and tapped the monitor, leaving a smudge. "You made the field private. That word you typed. So the test can't touch it." He read the error message twice, moving his lips on the second pass. "A field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class." He'd copied that line off the whiteboard on Tuesday, into the margins of his notebook, and apparently it had stuck. "The test is in a different class. It's outside looking in."

Eli sat back. From the living room, through the wall, came the murmur of his mother's television, some cooking show where the audience sighed in a long diminuendo every time somebody lifted a lid. He turned his pencil over and over on the table without noticing he was doing it. He had thought private was a kind of decoration, a formality, the way you might initial a page to show you'd read it. He hadn't understood that it was a wall with a door in it, and that the door was the getter.

"The getter," he said. He scrolled up to the method he'd written without much thought, the one called getTitle. "So the test has to knock. It can't just walk in."

"If you even wrote the getter right," Kaiden said. "Nobody checks those."

Eli deleted the broken line and typed myBook.getTitle instead, both parentheses, both quotes, the way Ms. Kapoor chanted during warmups: method, open, close, semicolon. He ran it. The console printed the title in clean black letters, no red anywhere, and for a second neither of them said anything, the way you don't speak when the engine finally turns over.

"So private doesn't mean secret," Eli said slowly, testing the idea as much as the code. "Ms. Kapoor can still see it if she wants. It means only her code can. Only the class." He was aware he was talking partly to himself, and that Kaiden was already checking his phone, but the distinction felt worth saying out loud, because he'd held two wrong pictures of it in his head all week, and now he held one right one, and he wanted to keep it. "The getter is the only door."

"Then write your three tests and close the laptop before you break it again." Kaiden dropped into the other chair and pulled out his own homework. "My mom's making enchiladas if you want to stay. She made a whole pan because my brother's being hedonistic about his birthday, three cakes, I'm not kidding."

Eli laughed and turned back to the screen. He wrote two more tests, one that read the title through the getter and one that changed it and read it back, and both of them ran green. Then he saved the file twice, because that was the kind of person he had decided to be. In the living room the audience sighed again as another lid came up, and somewhere down the street a garage door rattled shut. He left his cursor blinking after the last semicolon.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
Sofia's mother let her take the car on Sundays, when the driveway was empty of everything but the recycling bins. She had measured out a space between the bins with a tape measure: seven metres, the length the test required for parallel parking. For three Sundays Sofia had backed into it, crept forward, corrected, corrected again, and climbed out to look at her work with the sense that she was improving at something no one would ever applaud.

Ariel came by on the fourth Sunday, carrying a thermos and a laminated sheet of driving tips she had printed at the library. "Zayne says his cousin failed twice on the highway part," Ariel said, settling onto the front step. "Both times on merging."

"I haven't even been on the highway."

"That's my point." Ariel held up the sheet. On it, under a heading about lane changes, someone had written a single line in marker, like an epigram: "The mirror lies." Sofia read it, decided it was the kind of thing Zayne's cousin would write, and handed it back.

Her mother came out with the keys and her purse, on her way to the bank. "Take it up to the ring road if you're feeling ready," she said. "Stay under the limit. And don't spend anything, we're impecunious this month." She said the word lightly, but Sofia knew it was accurate; the insurance quote had been taped to the fridge for two weeks, waiting.

They drove the residential streets first, Ariel navigating from the passenger seat with exaggerated authority, and Sofia parallel parked twice more, once well and once with a bumper-adjacent moment that made them both go quiet. Then the streets widened, the lights grew further apart, and the entrance ramp to the ring road appeared on the right with a yellow sign showing two lanes converging.

Sofia accelerated up the ramp, signalling, watching the side mirror for traffic in the right lane. The mirror was empty. She began to steer left.

Ariel said her name once, sharply, and Sofia turned her head to look over her shoulder and there was a grey sedan, close, filling the lane that the mirror had shown her nothing of. She pulled the wheel back straight, held her line, and let the sedan pass before she moved over. Her hands were steady on the wheel but her breathing was not.

"The mirror lies," Ariel said.

"That's not what it is," Sofia said, and she meant it as a correction, not a slogan. The mirror had not lied; it simply could not show everything. There were blind spots beside and behind the car, whole zones the glass left out, and the only remedy was to turn and look. She merged on the second attempt, clean, and drove two exits and back with the radio off, thinking that the whole business rested on something odd: the machine gave you partial information, and the habit of checking what it couldn't tell you was what underpinned every safe lane change. Not speed, not nerve. A quick look over the shoulder, before you moved.

Back on their own street she performed the best parallel park of her life, ending four inches from the curb, and sat for a moment with the engine running, pleased in a private way she did not announce.

Ms. Lau, who lived at the corner and had watched four Sundays of this from her garden, walked over with her pruning shears and leaned in at the window. "Very nice," she said. "You know, I sat my test in 1989 and I still check over my shoulder every single time. Habit of a lifetime."

"Good," Sofia said. "That's what I'm building."

She pulled forward into the driveway to turn the car around, checked her mirror, signalled, and was halfway into her reverse when her mother's car swung around the bins and into the space Sofia had just left, no signal, no shoulder check, in a single unhurried motion.

"Love," her mother called through the open window, "you left the keys in it."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
Eric had his first paycheque folded into the back pocket of his jeans all morning, and by the time he reached business class he had memorized the top line and the bottom line and the ugly distance between them. Gross pay, five hundred and twelve dollars. Net pay, four hundred and six. Somewhere in a small grey box on that stub, a hundred and six dollars had been taken from him before he ever touched it.

Mr. Siddiqui had set up the day's work on the projector: a mock tax return, line by line, the kind students filled in as if they were twenty-six and renting an apartment. Eric sat between Karl and Rose and slid the paycheque out flat on the desk. Karl leaned over immediately, because Karl leaned over everything.

"You look like somebody stole your lunch," Karl said.

"Somebody did. Look. Federal tax, provincial tax, CPP, EI. Four deductions. I worked thirty hours at the arena and I got paid for twenty-four."

"It's not stolen," Rose said, not looking up from her own screen. "It's deferred. Some of it comes back at tax return time if they took too much. That's what the return is." Rose wanted the co-op placement at the accounting firm downtown more than she had ever wanted anything, and she had started speaking in whole paragraphs of financial vocabulary, as if the firm might somehow hear her.

"Deferred is a nice word for it," Eric said. "Money-now is money-now."

"Careful," Karl said, grinning. "That's a dysphemism. You're taking a neutral word and making it sound worse than it is. The opposite of a euphemism." He tapped the stub. "They're not robbers. They're deductions with names and percentages and a whole government website."

Eric pulled up his phone under the desk, where Mr. Siddiqui pretended not to see phones, and searched his pay stub line by line. The EI deduction, employment insurance. The CPP, the pension he would not touch for fifty years. Income tax withheld at an estimated rate, an estimate that assumed he earned this much every pay period all year, which he would not, because the arena cut hours in March. So some of the estimate would come back to him. Rose was right, and it annoyed him slightly how completely she was right.

Then he went looking for the other tax, the one you could see on every receipt, and this was where the afternoon turned strange. Karl had posted a photo in the class group chat of a receipt from his cousin's shop in Manchester: two coffees, a sandwich, a pastry, and a total with no tax line at all. Karl had captioned it "UK receipts are cleaner than ours, no tax, taxless, nothing."

Eric stared at the photo. He pulled up the Canadian receipt from his own lunch, where the sandwich was listed at one price and then HST was added at the bottom, an extra charge stacked on after the fact. The UK receipt showed nothing like that. Were sandwiches in Britain somehow untaxed?

"Mr. Siddiqui," Eric called across the room, "is there no sales tax in the UK? Karl says the receipt has no tax on it."

Mr. Siddiqui smiled the way he did when a student had almost stepped on something. "What do you think, Eric? Look it up. Tell us tomorrow."

Rose was already typing. "It's called VAT," she said. "Value added tax."

"Their sales tax is called VAT," Karl repeated, reading off his own screen now. "And it says here the standard rate has been twenty percent since January 4, 2011." He sat back. "Twenty percent. And built into the prices. It's in the sandwich price already. That's why the receipt looks clean."

"Wait," Eric said. His pen was moving on the back of the handout, working it. He wrote the UK sandwich price and took twenty percent of it, then wrote his Canadian price and added thirteen percent on top. The British tax was higher and yet invisible, folded into the shelf price like salt into dough. The Canadian tax was lower and always arrived at the till as a surprise. "So Karl's whole caption is backwards. It's not taxless. It's more taxed, just hidden."

"Hidden isn't quite fair either," Rose said. "It's disclosed differently. You could argue built-in pricing is more honest, because the price you see is the price you pay."

"Or less honest," Karl said, "because you never feel it leave."

Eric wrote both sentences down, one under the other, and looked at them. He had spent the morning feeling robbed by his paycheque, and now he was holding two ideas that pulled against each other: the tax you see and resent, and the tax you don't see and therefore don't resent. Which one was he supposed to prefer? He genuinely did not know. He liked knowing what things cost before he agreed to buy them. He also liked knowing, at the till, exactly how much of his money was going to the government, the way his paycheque had told him line by line, brutally, to the penny. Maybe both were tenable positions. Maybe the visible tax was the price of resentment and the hidden tax was the price of peace, and every country just picked its poison.

"There's no clean answer, is there," he said out loud. "You either see it and hate it, or you don't see it and forget it."

"That's the assignment," Mr. Siddiqui said from the front, not having heard any of it and somehow having heard all of it. "Opinions with evidence, Friday."

Rose closed her laptop with the click of someone who had just won something. "I'm doing mine on payroll deductions. The co-op firm loves payroll."

Eric folded his paycheque along its old crease and slid it back into his pocket, four hundred and six dollars of net truth, then picked up his pen and crossed out Karl's caption on the handout where he'd copied it. Underneath it he wrote: not taxless, just quieter.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
I am not, generally, someone who forwards things. That is what I told Clara the night she sent me the video, and it was mostly true, if you don't count the missing-cat poster from March, or the speech about the school board, or the clip of the gymnast falling off the beam that I sent to eleven people. The video Clara sent showed a flooded street, cars bobbing like corks, a man on a roof waving a shirt. Someone had captioned it "downtown this morning." Clara wanted me to pass it on to the group chat, and I wanted to, because it was terrifying and terrifying things feel important to circulate, which is exactly the logic I would later learn to distrust.

I was at my mother's office that Saturday because our apartment was being fumigated and I had nowhere else to sit with my homework. Her desk was in a corner near the window, and a colleague of hers, a quiet man named Mr. Leung from the floor above, had come down to borrow her monitor. I remembered him vaguely from the winter party, the one who had argued with my mother about whether the building's art counted as art at all. My mother called him an aesthete behind his hand, approvingly, as if that settled the matter. He was, my mother said, obdurate about beauty, which I understood to mean he would not back down about it, and I admired that without knowing why.

While he waited for something to load, I had Clara's video open on my phone. I must have made a sound, or my face did, because he glanced over. "That flood?" he said. "Everyone's posting it. My sister sent it at six this morning." He turned his own laptop toward me a little, not to teach me anything, only because he was doing it anyway. On his screen there was a browser plugin, already installed, and he fed the video's link into it. "InVID-WeVerify," he said, tapping the icon. "The project was funded by the European Union."

What happened next looked like magic and was not. The plugin split the video into key frames, still images lifted out of the moving water, the man on the roof, the cars, the drowned sign at the corner. He dragged one of the frames into a reverse image search the way you'd drag a file into a folder. A grid of results came up. The same man, the same shirt, the same street, dated three years ago, on a different continent. I sat very still.

"I did check things," I said, though when I thought back honestly, what I had checked, ever, was whether the person who sent me something was someone I liked. That had been my entire verification process, and I had predicate faith in it, the kind that rests on nothing you could name. "I usually look at the comments," I offered. He shrugged, not unkindly. "Comments tell you what people felt," he said. "Not when it happened." Then his print job finished and he went upstairs, and I was alone with the key frames.

I installed the plugin myself, at my mother's desk, with her password sticky note as my only obstacle. I pulled the flood video apart frame by frame, and I found, in the seventh one, a shop sign I could actually read, and I searched it, and it was in a town I had to look up twice because I hadn't heard of it once. The flood had been real. That was the part that unsettled me most. The water had been real, the man had been real, his wet shirt had been real, and the video was still a lie, because of a caption, because of "this morning," because terror travels faster than correction and nobody reverse-searches their own outrage.

I texted Clara before I could lose my nerve. She replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later, "how did you even find that," and I started to explain and stopped, because the explanation sounded like homework, and because part of me wanted to keep it, the way you keep a good secret. I told her anyway, mostly. I left out the part where I had already forwarded the gymnast clip to eleven people without a thought, because I was still narrating myself as someone careful, and the evidence was inconvenient.

The cost arrived quietly, later that night. The group chat moved on, as it does, to someone's birthday plans, and I noticed I was scrolling differently now, checking dates before I laughed, pausing before I sent, and the pausing made me slower, more apart from the others, like a person reading subtitles at a party. Some of the wonder was gone too. When Claire sent a clip of a whale swimming down a flooded avenue, gorgeous and impossible, I ran it through the frames before I let myself want it to be true. It was from a video game. I closed my laptop and sat in my mother's empty office, in the blue light of her sleeping monitor, and put my hand flat on the desk where the key frames had been.

"Still downtown this morning," I said to nobody, and turned off the lamp.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.
story:
Maelle had the laptop on the coffee table and the TV remote pushed aside like something she had outgrown, though she had reached for it ten minutes ago before catching herself. On the screen were two tables: CUSTOMERS, with its tidy rows of names, and ORDERS, with its customer IDs and amounts. The tutorial wanted her to find which customers had never ordered anything, and the solution, when she peeked at it, looked like this: SELECT customers.name FROM customers LEFT JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id WHERE orders.id IS NULL. She understood every word separately. Together they defeated her.

Alissa was sprawled on the couch with her feet on the armrest, nominally studying for a chemistry test, actually narrating her own loquacious internal monologue about whether Mr. Ba would curve the last quiz. "He won't," Maelle said, mostly to forestall the next ten minutes of it. "He curves nothing. He thinks suffering builds character." Alissa made a wounded sound and went back to highlighting, and Maelle went back to the join.

What bothered her was not the syntax. It was the shape of the thing. Why tables at all? She had imagined databases as something more organic, a web maybe, threads connecting to threads, and instead the tutorial kept insisting on this rigid grid, rows and columns like an endless spreadsheet. She said as much aloud, and Beau, who had been silently building a tower out of the coasters, looked up. "Why does it matter what shape it is if it works?" he said.

"It matters because I can't remember what I don't understand," she said. "I memorized the whole periodic table in tenth grade and lost it in a month. The stuff I actually get, I keep."

She opened a new tab and typed the question plainly: why are databases made of tables. The answer came back faster than she expected, and it landed strangely. The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." She read the sentence twice. Someone had invented this. Tables were not some natural law of computers; they were one man's argument, published the year her mother was born, about the best way to hold large amounts of shared information. She remembered Mr. Ba saying something once about how every system in a school, the bell schedule, the seating charts, the attendance sheets, was a set of choices someone had made and everyone else had inherited. She had rolled her eyes at the time. She did not roll them now.

"Listen to this," she said, and read the sentence aloud, the title of the paper with its strange grave formality, "for Large Shared Data Banks." Beau laughed at the word banks. "Data banks," he said. "Like data is money."

"Kind of like data is money," Maelle said slowly, and then something shifted. A LEFT JOIN was not a command to memorize; it was a way of saying, keep every person on the left, whether or not anything on the right claims them. The customers with nothing were still there, matched against a silence. She had been thinking of the query as a machine. It was closer to a question about who gets counted when nothing is recorded.

She tried it on the sample database. The query ran, and four names came back, including a customer named R. Okafor who had registered three years earlier and never bought a thing. Alissa leaned over the arm of the couch to look. "That's sad," she said. "They signed up and just never came back."

"Or they came back a hundred times and never ordered," Maelle said. "The table doesn't say." That was the part she kept turning over, that the query was honest in a way she hadn't expected: it told you exactly who was missing and nothing about why. She thought of her own yearbook messages from June, half of them from people she barely knew, promising to keep in touch, and how the database of her life would show a quiet gap where the friendship should have been, no column for the reason. She saved the query with a filename she almost immediately regretted, then didn't bother changing: maelle_gets_it.sql.

Beue had rebuilt his coaster tower to four levels. "So do you get it now?"

"Get it or memorized it," she said. "Ask me in a month." She closed the lid halfway, then opened it again and ran the query once more, watching the four empty-handed names fill the screen.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
Riley had written "Works Cited" at the top of the last page before he remembered, and by then the ink had dried into the blue line of the notebook paper. He sat in the back of Ms. Desir's history class with the draft flat under his hand, listening to her describe the research paper one more time: an argument, evidence, sources listed at the end. Last semester, in English, he had done all of this differently, or so it seemed now, and the habit of that class had followed him into this one the way a smell follows a coat out of a restaurant.

At lunch he spread the draft across the table in the library and stared at the heading. Jaeden dropped his bag into the chair across from him and unwrapped a sandwich without asking what was wrong, which meant he already knew.

"You did it again," Jaeden said.

"I did it again." Riley turned the page around so Jaeden could see. In English, their teacher had drilled the format until it felt somatic, something the hands did on their own: quote, then parentheses with the author's last name and the page number, then all the full sources gathered at the end of the paper under "Works Cited." Riley's fingers had learned it the way they had learned to tie shoes. He had stopped thinking about it months ago, and that was exactly the problem, because Ms. Desir had not asked for that.

"Fix the heading," Jaeden said through the sandwich. "She wants a bibliography. Just write 'Bibliography.'"

"That's it? Just change the word?"

"For the heading, yeah." Jaeden shrugged and brushed crumbs off the table. "The rest, I don't know. She never told us to put author and page in parentheses. History people just seem to want things their own way."

Riley looked down at the body of the paper, where the little parenthetical citations sat at the ends of his sentences like small closed doors. Some of them held only page numbers, because he had mentioned the author's name in the sentence itself, which his English teacher had praised as smooth. He could not tell anymore whether the smoothness was good or whether it was just a style, one dialect among several, and Ms. Desir happened to speak a different one. It occurred to him that the format was not trying to inculcate some deep truth about the past; it was a convention, an agreement, no more moral than driving on one side of the road. What mattered was that everyone on the road had agreed.

Vivienne arrived late, hair still wet from gym, and slid into the seat beside him. She had the same assignment, and she wanted the grade more than she wanted the paper; she had said so twice that week, once flatly and once as a joke, and Riley had laughed both times because refusing to would have cost something. Now she leaned over his pages and read faster than seemed fair.

"Your in-text stuff is done," she said. "Author, page, parentheses, all of it. Can I see your source list before class?" She said it lightly, the way you ask for a pencil, and Riley almost slid the last page across before he understood what she was asking for. She didn't want the format. She wanted the sources, the whole compiled list at the end, so she would not have to build her own.

"That's the part I did," he said.

"I'll change the order." She was already reaching.

He put his hand flat on the page. Through the window behind her, two groundskeepers were moving a goalpost across the far field, lifting and walking, lifting and walking, and he watched them for a second because it was easier than watching her face. He had his own history with borrowed work, small things, and he knew the difference between helping and disappearing into someone else's deadline, though the discernment came slower than the anger did.

"You can look at how I did the citations," he said. "You can't have the list. I'll sit with you while you build yours."

Vivienne took her hand back and looked at the table. "Fine," she said. "Whatever." But she pulled out a stack of photocopied pages she had clearly been carrying around for days, and when Riley tapped one and asked where she'd found it, she started telling him, quickly at first and then with real attention, about a mill strike she had found on the third page of an archive scan. He picked up his pen and crossed out "Works Cited," writing "Bibliography" above it, and then, on a clean sheet, began copying the heading for her.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Charoset, a sweet paste of chopped fruit and nuts on the Seder plate, represents the mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt.
story:
The notebook lay open on the kitchen counter between a bag of walnuts and three bruised apples, and Alexia had written nothing in it for ten minutes. Her grandmother, who had led the Seder for thirty-one years, was in Arizona visiting her sister and would not be back in time, and her mother had said, with a strange lightness that Alexia recognized as fear disguised as a joke, that maybe this year someone else would have to know what to do. That someone was her. She was sixteen, and she had never so much as set the table without being told where the forks went.
