Then he stood at the counter stirring the sauce and argued with himself. The study implied a strategy: mirror her. If she leaned forward, lean forward. If she tucked her hair back, wait a beat and tuck his own hair back, which was short, which would look like a tic. He could not decide whether using the trick was clever or whether it was a small dishonesty, a fake version of the attentiveness he actually felt. It was one thing to be altruistic with your attention, he thought, and another to spend it on calculations.

She arrived at six wearing a green jacket, holding a bag of the expensive bread from the shop near the library. "I panicked at the register," she said. "The cashier asked if I wanted it sliced and I said no, and now we have to tear it like medieval people." He laughed, genuinely, and the knot in his chest loosened by one careful degree.

The first course went well. He did not mimic anything. He asked about her brothers, she asked about the talent show, and he told the story against himself, which made her laugh so hard she had to put her fork down. But somewhere during the pasta, he noticed something that stopped him mid-sentence. She had leaned onto her elbows, forearms on the table, chin propped on her laced fingers. And he was leaning onto his elbows, forearms on the table, chin propped on his laced fingers. He had not done it first. He was sure of that. Or almost sure.

His pulse went strange and quick. He tested it, slowly, the way you test ice. He let one hand drift down to the table edge. Twenty seconds later, so smoothly he could have imagined it, her hand drifted down too. He took a sip of water. She took a sip of water. The kitchen clock ticked through it. He felt like he was watching weather happen inside the room, something vast and invisible that nonetheless had a rhythm, and he could not tell whether he was inside it or outside it, whether the study was happening to them or whether he was inventing the pattern out of nerves, the way people see faces in the grain of a ceiling.

"Okay," she said, putting her glass down. "You're doing a psychology thing."

He went still. "What?"

"Your friend Aryanna texted me an hour before I came over. She said, and I quote, 'He read a study about mimicry, don't let him use it on you.' She was trying to protect me, I think, or protect you from yourself." Angelie's expression was hard to read, somewhere between amused and something cooler. "But here's the thing, Sebastian. I was doing it to you first. Since the bread. I saw you lean on your elbows and I copied it, and then you copied me copying you, and honestly I lost track of who started."

The silence had weight. He looked at his plate, then at her, and decided, in that moment, to give up the calculation entirely, not because it was wrong but because he could no longer locate its edges. "So which one of us is the 1999 study working on right now?"

She considered this with mock seriousness, tapping her chin. "Unclear," she said. "The data is contaminated." Then she reached across the tablecloth and tore the medieval bread in half, and handed him the larger piece.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
The gown came back from Emmy's house smelling of her mother's fabric softener, and Elliot hung it on the closet door where it swayed whenever the air conditioning kicked on. He had worn it once, for the yearbook photo, and had felt ridiculous then, a neophyte in costume, but his mother had already framed that picture and set it on the mantel beside the invitation. Forty people were coming. His father had spent the morning arranging folding chairs in the backyard and had not said much about any of it.

"You could talk to him," Emmy said. She was sitting on the porch steps with her own gown crumpled in her lap, eating grapes out of the bag she'd brought because she claimed his house never had food. "Or you could just not talk to him. Those are your options, basically."

"He'll bring it up himself. He brings everything up himself."

At dinner, his uncle did bring it up. He set down his fork, looked down the length of the table at Elliot, and said, "You know what that diploma's worth? In 2023, workers twenty-five and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars. Without one, seven hundred and eight." He let the numbers sit there among the potato salad. "That's the difference. Every week."

"I know how math works," Elliot said.

"Don't be smart with him," his mother said, but his father had already put down his plate. He had left school in eleventh grade and never litigated the decision with anyone, not even when the family had tried to. He had worked warehouses, then heating and air, and now he owned half of a company with two vans and his name painted on the side. "Median," his father said quietly. "You know what that means, right? Half the people are under it."

"I know what it means," his uncle said. "It's still eight ninety-nine against seven-oh-eight."

The argument went the way Elliot had expected, which was nowhere. His uncle recited the numbers again as though repetition were proof, and his father said, "You're comparing people, not diplomas," and his uncle called that specious, which his father clearly took as an insult though it was meant, technically, as a description. Elliot watched them both and found he could see each man's side at the same time, which was an uncomfortable way to stand, like balancing on a fence rail. The numbers were real. His uncle hadn't invented them. And his father wasn't a statistic, and the money his father earned now came from twenty years of crawl spaces and frozen fingers, none of which showed up in a median. Both things were true and they did not fit together, and everyone at the table wanted him to pick one and hold it up like a sign.

He didn't pick. He carried the folding chairs back to the garage instead, stacking them two at a time, and his father followed him with the last row and stood in the doorway with one chair still in his hands.

"You're going in the fall," his father said. It wasn't a question.

"Yeah."

"Good." His father set the chair down on the stack, badly, so that it slid, and he caught it and reseated it, aligning the legs with a care that the chair did not deserve. "You don't have to say anything about all that in there."

"I wasn't going to."

That night, after the last of the relatives' cars had pulled out, Elliot found a message on his phone from Emmy, sent at 9:14 while he'd been washing dishes. "Leaving early, sorry. My dad did the same speech at my house except he added the part about how I should thank him personally for my future earnings. Barrett said his uncle used the exact same numbers, so I think they're all reading the same website. Anyway. You looked good up there. Text me when the yard is clean."

He read it twice, then stood at the kitchen window with the phone warm in his hand, looking out at the dark backyard where the chairs had been. Somewhere past the fence his father's work van sat in the driveway with its peeling letters. Elliot typed, deleted, typed again.

"You want to come over tomorrow and help me take the lights down?" he wrote, and pressed send, and watched the screen for the three dots.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
The envelope from the university had been on the kitchen table for three days, and Joshua had opened it exactly once, to confirm that the housing deposit was six hundred dollars and due on the fifteenth. Six hundred was also, as it happened, the balance in the shoebox under his bed, accumulated over two summers of pushing a mower through the neighborhood, and tonight at nine o'clock a limited run of the console he had wanted since eighth grade would go on sale for five hundred and eighty. He sat on his bedroom floor with the shoebox in his lap and did not open it, because opening it would make the arithmetic real.

Downstairs, his mother was on the phone with somebody from the open house they had gone to last weekend, a woman whose son was also starting in the fall. Joshua could hear only his mother's half of it as he came down for a glass of water. "No, I hadn't either. She said there was a follow-up in 1990 of the preschoolers from Mischel's study, the ones who waited for the second treat, and the kids who had waited longer tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers." A pause. "I don't know, I'd have to look it up. Her husband's a psychologist, apparently." His mother laughed at something, and Joshua stood at the sink longer than he needed to, holding the glass.

He looked it up himself, later, on the slow laptop in the den. The study was real. Preschoolers, one treat now or two later, and a 1990 follow-up that found the longer waiters tended, as teenagers, toward higher SAT scores. He read the sentence twice and then closed the lid, because the sentence was looking back at him. One afternoon with a marshmallow, and the story it apparently told about you at seventeen. He was seventeen, and in six hours a countdown clock on a retail website would hit zero, and the whole thing felt like a test someone had left on the table while they left the room.

It wasn't as though he hadn't waited before. He had waited through two birthdays and one Christmas without asking for the console, had acclimated to not having it the way you acclimate to a house that's colder than you'd like, by wearing another layer and mostly forgetting. But this was different, he told himself. This was a limited run. This wasn't patience being tested; it was scarcity. The preschoolers in the study weren't staring at a discontinued item. He wrote that argument on a sticky note, in a sense, and then argued back: the researchers hadn't said what kind of reward it was. Only that you could have more of it later, or less of it now.

He went out the back door without deciding anything, just to move. Mr. Kelly was on his patio with a tray of seedlings, a species of montane pine he'd ordered from a nursery in Colorado, and he was spooning gritty substrate around each root ball with a teaspoon. "These things take ten years to look like anything," Mr. Kelly said, not looking up. "Fifteen before they're worth photographing." He pressed the soil with his thumb. "You want to help me carry the tray into the garage? Frost tonight."

They carried it together, forty small pots, and Mr. Kelly talked about elevation zones and how these trees spent their first years looking like nothing at all. Joshua asked why he bothered, and Mr. Kelly said, "Because I'd like to be the kind of person who has montane pines when he's seventy-five, and there's no way to become that person late." It wasn't a lecture; it was barely even an answer. But Joshua stood in the garage with his hands dirty and the words settled somewhere under his ribs, the way the substrate settled around the roots.

At 8:41 his phone buzzed. Caden: "drop is in 19 min. you in? i can only cover half, you'd need the rest by 9." Joshua typed back that the money was spoken for, sort of, maybe. Caden replied with a photo of the product page and the words "when is it EVER spoken for." Joshua sat on the porch steps and typed, deleted, and typed again. "housing deposit. due the 15th." There was a long pause, long enough that he watched a moth make four circuits of the porch light. Then Caden: "ok that's actually fair. resell later when we both have jobs. deal?" Joshua wrote "deal," and something in his chest went slack with relief and tight with loss at the same moment, and he didn't try to name which one was winning.

At nine he did not open the website. He put the shoebox money into an envelope, counted it twice, sealed it, and wrote the university's address on the front in his careful printing. His mother came through the kitchen, saw the envelope, and put her hand briefly on his shoulder on her way to the refrigerator. She didn't say anything. From the driveway came the sound of Mr. Kelly dragging his frost cloth across the yard, an unhurried scraping.

Caden texted at 9:20: "got mine. it's beautiful. hate you a little." Joshua smiled at the screen and then set the phone face-down. Later, lying awake, he thought about the follow-up study and how it only said tended to, which was not the same as would, and he thought about how nobody had followed up to see whether the kids who waited were happier, or lonelier, or whether any of them had wanted the marshmallow so badly it still ached at forty. He had made his choice and he believed it was the sound one, and he honestly could not tell whether the belief or the ache was going to last longer. On the desk beside his bed, the sealed envelope sat white in the dark. In the garage, forty small pines waited out the frost.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: In most jurisdictions traffic already on a highway has the right of way, so a merging driver must adjust speed to fit a gap rather than expect others to make room.
story:
Jake had spent the whole of Sunday afternoon in the driveway with a book called Pass Your Test the First Time, and by evening he could recite the steps of parallel parking the way other people recited song lyrics. His father came out around five, looked at the book propped against the wheel, and asked whether Jake wanted to actually drive or just memorize the idea of driving. Jake said he wanted to pass. His father went back inside without commenting, which was its own kind of comment.

The test was in eleven days. The driving school had one car and a waiting list, so his father had agreed to take him out in the family sedan on weeknights, after dinner, when the streets of their subdivision went quiet. The arrangement felt fragile. His father worked long hours and treated every mistake behind the wheel as a small accusation, and Jake had learned to compartmentalize the evenings: the drives were a separate drawer in his head, opened at seven, shut at eight.

They started with cones borrowed from Gordon, who lived two streets over and had cones because his older brother had failed the test twice and had left the equipment behind when he moved out for good. Gordon came out to watch the first attempt, standing on the curb with his hands in his pockets like a man watching a dock being unloaded. Jake pulled alongside the imaginary car, reversed, cut the wheel, straightened, and stopped a full meter from the curb.

"That's a parking spot for a bus," Gordon said.

His father said nothing, which was worse. Jake pulled out and tried again, and again, and on the sixth attempt his rear tire kissed the curb with a sound like a knuckle rapping a table. His father exhaled through his nose. Gordon, trying to be useful, said that his brother had failed for exactly that, and Jake told him to be quiet, and then apologized, and then did it again.

By Thursday he could park in three tries out of four. The improvement had a texture to it he hadn't expected: each successful attempt felt less like triumph and more like the removal of a weight he'd grown used to carrying. He understood now why his brother-in-law, who had taken up running, described the first mile as the worst one. The reward for competence was that you stopped noticing the fear, which meant you also stopped noticing the fear leaving.

The highway was a different matter. The on-ramp near their house was short and curved, and at the top of it the traffic came fast, and Jake's instinct, every time, was to freeze and hope. On Friday night a semi-truck filled his mirror as he reached the merge, and he slowed, hovering in the acceleration lane with his heart going, waiting for the truck to slide left and let him in.

His father's voice came low and even. "Who has to yield here, Jake? Him or you?"

"I don't know. Him? He's got room."

"Traffic already on the highway has the right of way. In most jurisdictions, that's the rule. The merging driver adjusts. Not the other way around."

The ramp was running out. Jake looked at the gap behind the truck, lifted his speed, and slid into it, and the car shuddered slightly as he straightened, and then it was done and they were doing a hundred and ten and nothing had happened. His hands were shaking anyway. "So I was waiting for the world to move for me," he said.

"That's one way of putting it," his father said, and turned the radio down a notch, though it had barely been on.

Jake thought about it for the next three kilometers, the strip malls and storage yards sliding past. The rule felt unfair and then, gradually, felt like something else. The driver of the truck didn't know him, owed him nothing, had his own schedule and his own blind spots. It wasn't unkindness. It was just the design. He tested the thought out loud, carefully, the way you'd step on ice. "So the whole thing is, you fit yourself into what's already moving."

"Off the ramp, yes," his father said. "Life off the ramp, I'm not answering."

On Saturday, Kaitlin from his homeroom texted to ask if he'd passed yet, and he told her the truth, that he hadn't even taken it, and she replied that she'd failed her first attempt on the parallel parking and had cried in the test centre parking lot while her mother sat beside her saying nothing. Somehow the message made him feel better and worse at once. He sat on the front steps with the phone in his hand, watching the street where, someday soon, he would be allowed to drive alone, and the prospect had the same strange quality as her text: a door opening onto a room he couldn't fully see.

That night he reviewed the handbook at the kitchen table, an ascetic little ritual now, no music, no phone, just the pages and a glass of water, and he noticed that the merge section said exactly what his father had said, and that he'd read it weeks ago and retained nothing, because reading it and doing it were two different countries. He closed the book and looked out the window at the parked sedan, rear tire a hand's width from the curb, where his father had left it, perfect, effortless, the way it had been parked his whole life without Jake ever once considering the geometry of it.

Monday evening they went out again. The subdivision was quiet and Gordon was on his curb, and this time Jake didn't look at him. He pulled alongside the cone, checked his mirror, reversed, cut the wheel, and felt the car settle against the curb on the first try, so smoothly that for a second he didn't trust it. He sat there with the engine running and his hands loose on the wheel.

"How was that?" his father asked.

Jake looked at the tire, then at the road ahead, where the on-ramp waited somewhere past the last streetlight. "Ask me on the highway," he said, and put the car in drive.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In NLRB v. J. Weingarten (1975), the US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline.
story:
The letter had come in the afternoon mail, and it lay beside the salt now while the three of them ate, face down, as though turning it over might change what it said. Chase's father had mentioned it once, in the driveway, in the flat voice he saved for the hospital: a meeting tomorrow morning, nine sharp, with the food service manager and someone from administration. Then he had carried the grocery bags inside and said nothing else.

"Your grandmother's tomatoes came in," his mother said, spooning the last of the salad onto Chase's plate. "Six of them. She's calling them autochthonous now, because some word-of-the-day calendar told her that means they're from here, native to the place. She's very proud." She was a night nurse at the same hospital, and she talked about her day the way she always did, in pieces: a patient with a fever, a rash nobody could source, an antigen test run twice because the first result made no sense. Chase liked hearing it, and tonight he needed the sound of ordinary things.

"Is it about the schedule thing?" he asked his father. "The swap you did for Delores in July?"

His father cut his chicken with more attention than the chicken required. "They said an interview. Not a meeting. Interview's the word they used."

Chase's heart began to palpitate, a quick uneven drumming he could feel in his throat, and he set his fork down. Two weeks ago he would have said go in, answer straight, you did nothing wrong. He had thought that way all summer at the hardware store, where he'd been written up for a register shortage he hadn't counted and had sat alone in the back office while the manager read the numbers aloud, slowly, like a verdict. No one had told him he could have anyone with him. Whether anyone would have come, whether it would have mattered, he still didn't know. The store wasn't union. Nobody there even said the word as far as he'd heard.

But the hospital kitchen was. He knew that from Sahil, whose mother was a steward, and it was Sahil he had texted from the porch an hour ago, thumbing fast, and Sahil who had called back and talked for eleven minutes while the mosquitoes found Chase's ankles.

"Dad," Chase said. "At lunch today Sahil told me about a case. NLRB v. J. Weingarten, 1975. The US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline." He had said it back to Sahil twice on the phone to make sure he had it right, because Sahil's mother had drilled it into him, and because Sahil had laughed at Chase's first attempt, when Chase had claimed it covered any worker at any meeting, which it didn't, and Sahil had corrected him gently, the way you correct someone who is about to use a fact where it doesn't fit.

His father looked up. "You're union," Chase said. "At the hospital. You're a unionized worker." He felt the strange double weight of it, that a thing he'd gotten wrong at four o'clock he was handing over corrected at seven, and that his father, fifty-three years old, thirty of them in that kitchen, might not know it either. Or might know it and have decided, some other hard year, that asking for a rep made you look guilty, made you a problem, and had filed that decision away where Chase couldn't reach it.

His mother had stopped eating. "Frank, call the steward tonight," she said. "Before the meeting. Not at nine tomorrow with your heart going like his is now."

His father's jaw moved. For a moment Chase thought he would say what he sometimes said about the local, that the dues came out of every check whether you needed them or not, that he'd never once called. Instead he pushed his plate back, went to the hall, and came back with the phone and a folded paper from the drawer where the warranty manuals lived. He dialed the number printed under the union's letterhead and stood at the edge of the table, not leaving the room, not quite joining it.

"Tom?" he said into the phone. "It's Frank, third floor kitchens. Yeah, it's been a while." He turned the letter over and set it on the table between the salt and the salad bowl so they could all see the letterhead, the administrator's name, the word interview. "I've got a sit-down tomorrow morning, and I think I'd like somebody sitting next to me."

His mother reached across and took the last tomato, his grandmother's autochthonous one, and ate it slowly while the phone crackled.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The house smelled of cold dust and lemon polish, and Amy stood in her grandmother's kitchen holding a tin box of recipe cards, deciding what to take. The funeral had been two days ago. Her mother was in the bedroom sorting sweaters into boxes marked donate and keep, and her father was out by the shed taking photographs of tools so they could be sold. Nobody had told Amy what her job was, so she had given herself the kitchen.

The cards were soft at the corners, written in her grandmother's looping hand. One said simply, "Chicken, the good way." Another was for a honey cake with a note in the margin: "Underbake it, they always say it's dry, it isn't." Amy put five cards in her coat pocket, then took two out, then put them back. She wasn't sure what the rule was, whether she was allowed to want them this much.

Kylan arrived at four with a box of her grandmother's dishes his mother had bought at the estate sale, saying his mother wanted Amy to look through them first in case anything mattered. He set the box on the counter and looked at the wall where the calendar still hung on March. "Do you want me to stay?" he said. Amy said she didn't know, and he stayed anyway, sitting on the counter with his sneakers against the cupboard door, which her grandmother would have objected to.

Amy told him about the cards. She told him she'd been cooking from one the night after the funeral, in her own kitchen at home, and that halfway through the honey cake she had started explaining out loud why she was substituting oil for butter, telling her grandmother, as if her grandmother were standing at the stove with her. "And then I stopped," she said, "because it felt like something I should have grown out of."

Kylan turned his phone over in his hands. "My cousin took her grandfather's watch," he said. "Wears it every day. Nobody thinks that's weird." Amy said a watch was different, a watch was just an object, and this was talking to someone who wasn't there, which was either a habit or a problem. Kylan shrugged. "You could look it up," he said, in the flat tone he used when he thought she was making something harder than it was.

She looked it up while he washed the dishes nobody had asked him to wash. There was a book from 1996, by Dennis Klass and Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, called Continuing Bonds, and it argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who had died was a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on. She read the sentence twice, then read it aloud, and Kylan dried his hands and said, "Continuing bonds," testing the phrase, and went back to the dishes. Amy sat with her phone on the counter and felt the thin floor of what she'd believed shift under her, and she could not yet tell whether the new floor was solid.

She thought about her mother in the bedroom, who had cried exactly once, at the cemetery, and who had spent every evening since boxing things efficiently, as though grief were a task that could be finished if you worked steadily, as though she had something to expiate and the boxes were penance. And she thought about herself, keeping the cards, talking to the air. Two ways of carrying the same woman. She did not think one was braver than the other. She thought her mother's way looked like control and hers looked like weakness, and that maybe the looks were wrong in both directions, the way a photograph of the ocean shows a flat surface and misses the cold stratum moving underneath.

She took the honey cake card out of her pocket and set it on the counter where the flour always sat. In the yard, her father lowered the camera and stood without doing anything for a moment, and the garden was quiescent, the beans her grandmother had planted in May still climbing the strings she'd tied. Amy turned on the oven. She had butter this time. "Fine," she said to the empty kitchen, out loud, feeling ridiculous and not stopping. "Tell me about the pan." Kylan opened the drawer where the pans had always been, third from the left, and she greased it while the oven ticked up toward temperature.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act does not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors or independent contractors.
story:
The notice had been taped to the door of the union hall since Tuesday, and by Friday afternoon Liam had walked past it four times without going in. THIRD SHIFT WAGE VOTE, it said, MONDAY 7 PM. Below that, in smaller print, someone had added, ALL WELCOME. He had the folded flyer from the hardware store in his back pocket, the one his cousin had mailed him in June, the one that started all of this, and he stood on the cracked steps with the July heat pressing on his neck and tried to decide whether all welcome meant him.

Inside, the hall smelled of coffee and floor wax and something older, cigarette smoke soaked into the wood over decades. Folding chairs faced a low stage where a woman was taping a banner that read HARVEST SEASON, FAIR SEASON. That was Ms. Nair. He knew her from the grocery store, where she worked the register and called everyone by name, and she recognized him too.

"Liam. You're not third shift at the plant." She came down off the stage without asking how he knew that.

"No. I'm picking for Hollis Orchards this summer." He unfolded the flyer, which his cousin had circled in red ink: JOIN UP. GET IT IN WRITING. "My cousin works at the plant in Dayton. He kept saying I should get the same deal, seniority, overtime after forty, a grievance process. He made it sound simple. You sign, you're covered."

Ms. Nair looked at the flyer for a long moment, and he could see her choosing her words the way a person chooses footing on ice. "Who's your cousin's rep?"

"Brady. Brady Kowalski. He's home this week, actually." Liam had not called him. He had meant to, all week, but every time he picked up the phone he realized he did not know what he was asking.

Brady was outside by the pickup trucks ten minutes later, because Curtis had texted him, and Curtis texted everyone about everything. Curtis had texted Liam too: COME TO THE MEETING, FARM KID, YOU'LL LEARN SOMETHING. Brady leaned against the truck with his boots crossed and let Liam explain the flyer, the red circle, the whole summer of eleven-hour days hauling ladders in the sun for a flat day rate that never changed no matter how many hours the foreman called in.

"Okay," Brady said slowly, "so here's the thing, and I should have told you in June. The law we organize under, the National Labor Relations Act, it doesn't cover everybody. It doesn't cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors, or independent contractors." He held up his hand before Liam could speak. "Agricultural workers. That's you. That's the picking."

Liam stood there while a sprinkler across the parking lot ticked through its arc. "So when you said get it in writing."

"I meant my writing. My contract. I get overtime after forty hours because my plant bargained for it, and the law backs the bargaining. You don't even get the law. If Hollis fired you Monday for mentioning the word union, there'd be no case. It's not illegal the way it would be illegal for me." Brady's face had gone uncomfortable. "I expatiated on my contract for half an hour at your graduation party and never once thought about yours. That was careless. Honestly it was worse than careless. It's how the pernicious stuff survives, all of us assuming the rules are the same rules."

Inside, the meeting had started. Ms. Nair was reading the proposed wage schedule into the microphone, and the numbers came out clipped and clear, and people around the room marked their ballots with golf pencils. Liam sat in the back with Curtis, who whispered the local's history in his ear: the strike in the eighties, the winter they nearly lost the hall, the year the company tried to reclassify half the drivers as independent contractors and the local spent eight months proving they weren't. "That's the fight now," Curtis whispered. "Companies learn the loopholes faster than we close them."

Liam looked at the ballots going into the box and understood, with a feeling like a floor shifting under him, that everything around him in this room had been built, that eleven dollars an hour was not a fact of nature but a decision someone had won, and that the ladder he hauled through the orchard rows sat outside all of it, in the part of the world the law had never reached. He thought about arguing with Brady, pointing out that the picking crew had made noises about asking Hollis for shade and water breaks, that maybe something could still happen. He thought about the opposite, that maybe summer labor was supposed to be raw and temporary and he was borrowing a grievance that did not belong to him. Both thoughts felt true and he could not make them into one.

After the vote he found Ms. Nair stacking chairs. "Can I ask you something that isn't about the plant?"

"Ask."

"The Hollis crew. There's like nine of us, and Curtis says there used to be a farmworkers committee in this county, years back, before everything went quiet. If the federal law doesn't cover us, is there anything left that does? Anything we could actually do?" He heard how young the question sounded and kept going anyway. "I only have five weeks left before college. I know that."

Ms. Nair set the last chair on the stack and studied him with the same unhurried attention she gave a receipt that wouldn't add up. "There's a filing cabinet in the back room with the old committee papers. Nobody's opened it since I started here. Come Monday after the vote, before you head to the fields, and we'll pull the drawers."

"I'll be at the orchard at six," Liam said.

"Then come at five-thirty." She handed him the roll of banner tape, and he started pulling it down from the stage, the letters coming away one at a time in his hands.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
Jason had joined the book club for two reasons, only one of which he admitted to himself, and the second reason had brown hair and a way of arguing that made other people go quiet. They met on Tuesdays in the back room of the bookshop, seven folding chairs, a kettle, and a poster that said READ MORE, as if anyone there needed convincing. Tonight's text was Pride and Prejudice, and Mr. Pelletier, who ran the club and sold them their tea at cost, had written two words on the whiteboard: power and property.

"Mr. Pelletier wants us to try a critical lens," Lauren said, flipping to a marked page. "Like reading the book through a pair of glasses tinted with Marxism. Or feminism. He wants us to notice what the book takes for granted."

Jason had underlined a passage in pencil and then, dissatisfied, underlined it again in pen, so it looked like a small scar on the page. Mrs. Bennet was carrying on about Mr. Bingley's arrival in the neighborhood, five thousand a year, and Jason had written in the margin, hysterical? He had written it with a question mark because that was as far as his thinking had gone. He was seventeen and had spent most of his literary life deciding whether he liked characters, as if novels were restaurants.

Dominic, who read with a highlighter in three colors and treated this as unremarkable, leaned forward. "Okay, but here's the thing everyone skates past. The Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr. Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home." He said it flatly, a fact laid on the table like a receipt. "The house they live in belongs, basically, to a cousin they can't stand. When their father dies, they're out."

There was a pause while this went around the circle like something being passed hand to hand. Jason felt a small, atavistic alarm, the kind that comes from imagining one's own bedroom belonging to a stranger. Then he looked at his marginal note and understood, in one unglamorous motion, what he had missed. Mrs. Bennet was not a comic noise. She was a woman doing arithmetic.

"So her matchmaking," Jason said slowly, "is not her being ridiculous. It's her being the only person in the house with a savings plan." He was working it out as he spoke, which he disliked doing in public, though less than he used to. "If you read it through the money, the whole plot is about women trying to acquire, through marriage, the security the law won't let them inherit."

Lauren turned her copy around so he could see her own margin, where she had written the same idea more neatly in green ink. "And if you read it through the gender lens, it's the same fact wearing different clothes," she said. "Marxism and feminism keep arriving at the same door here. I don't know if that means they agree or if the house just happens to be at that address."

"That's the part that bothers me," Jason said. "When two lenses give you the same answer, you can't tell if you've found something true or if you've just found a coincidence." He had wanted, coming in, to leave with a conclusion, something he could carry like a coin in his pocket. What he had instead was a better question, which was heavier and less convenient.

Mr. Pelletier refilled the kettle without comment. He had a policy of letting the room ferment on its own, intervening only when someone was about to leave or when the tea ran out, and the tea was still going.

"Elizabeth refuses Mr. Collins," Dominic said, counting on his fingers, "and everyone acts as if her mother's reaction is the joke. But Mrs. Bennet isn't wrong that refusal has a price. She's just the only one willing to say the price out loud."

"Maybe that's the rapprochement," Lauren said. "Not between the lenses. Between Mrs. Bennet and us. We laughed at her for two hundred years and she was doing the math the whole time."

They argued about Wickham for a while, then about whether Charlotte Lucas was a cynic or a realist, and the argument did not resolve so much as get folded up with the chairs at nine o'clock. Outside, the street was wet and Jason walked with Lauren as far as the corner where their routes divided. He was still holding his book with the scarred page.

"I'm going to read it again," he said. "The whole thing. Looking for what else I laughed at."

"Bring the green pen next time," she said, and crossed the street.
